stops.name: The Round Table camp, Cundrie's curse and the renunciation of God
stops.campa: The feast is barely begun when Cundrie the sorceress rides into camp, hideous and learned, and curses Parzival before the whole Round Table by name: he sat beside the Grail king's suffering and never asked the healing word, and every honor just given him is void. She calls the knights instead to rescue the four queens held in Klingsor's enchanted Schastel Marveil, and rides off toward it. Parzival, shattered, turns to Gawain and disowns the God he has served since infancy, swearing to seek Him no more, then rides alone from the camp that welcomed him only hours before, into six years of wandering.
stops.quote: Woe is me! Who is He, this mighty God? Had He power, then methinks our portion had ne'er been this shame abhorred! Small power shall be His! I served Him from the day I first knew His grace, henceforth I renounce His service; doth He hate me, His hate I'll face!
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book VI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Parzival to Gawain

stops.name: Bearosche (Besançon), fighting on the wrong side
stops.campa: Within weeks of riding from the Birs, Parzival, still unknown by his blazon, finds himself before the walled, river-looped town of Bearosche, where Gawain has ridden to defend the townspeople against the besieging army of Meljanz. Parzival takes the field on the opposing side without recognizing his own new companion of the Round Table across the melee, one more proof that the God he has renounced has left him wandering blind even among friends. Neither man learns until much later how close their spears came that autumn under the walls of a town neither will remember naming the other.

stops.name: Schampfanzun (Champagnole), Vergulaht sent to the Grail quest
stops.campa: At Champagnole, seat of young King Vergulaht above the drained bed of an ancient Jura lake, Parzival defeats his host in single combat over an old grievance and, sparing him as he spared Kingrun and Clamide before, commits him instead to ride in search of the Grail he himself has lost. Neither man yet knows they share a grandfather, Gandin, or that this half-recognized cousin will later cross Parzival's road again through Kahenis of Punt. Parzival rides on, ignorant that Gawain will pass through this same town within days looking for the very same king.

stops.name: The fountain of Lac, at the source of the Larg
stops.campa: Four years and more of tournaments and joyless victories have cracked the sword Anfortas gave him at Munsalvaesche, the one weapon left of that whole ruined night. He remembers, at last, Sigune's old counsel, that the blade came from Trebuchet's forge and can be mended only at the spring called Lac, where a stream named Karnant rises among the Sundgau hills. He finds the source, presses the broken halves together in the running water, and draws out a sword whole and brighter than before, as if the years themselves could be rejoined as cleanly, though his own wound will need a harder cure.
stops.quote: The sword will withstand the first blow, at the next it will break in twain... Lac is the name of that fountain. If unsplintered shall be the blade, then press thou its halves together, from the waters shall it be made.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book V, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Sigune's instruction, fulfilled here

stops.name: Sigune's cell, the third meeting
stops.campa: On a Saturday in March, Parzival rides again between the two rock gates of Terre de salvaesche, still hunting the Grail Castle he cannot relocate on his own, and finds Sigune's cell for a third time. Six years have not softened her grief; her cousin's corpse still lies embalmed across her lap. But her rage at Parzival has cooled into pity, and she tells him plainly that Cundrie was here only a little before, that her mule stands always by the rock port where the waterfall gushes, and sends him after her tracks toward Munsalvaesche one more time.

stops.name: The Liten, the Templar's spear and the lost horse
stops.campa: Following Cundrie's mule-track up the rocky slope called the Liten, a crossroads Wolfram likens to a spider's web where a wrong turn is easily made, Parzival comes within sight of Munsalvaesche's outer line at last, only to be challenged by one of the Templeisen guarding the approach. Neither man yields; in the clash Parzival's own horse is killed under him. He mounts the Templar's instead and turns back into the forest, no closer to the door that shut on him six years before, but for the first time certain he is riding in the right country.

stops.name: Brizljan Forest in the snow, Kahenis of Punt
stops.campa: Cold returns hard over Brizljan Forest, ground white again as it was the day of the blood-drops, when Parzival meets a company of pilgrims on foot, barefoot in the frost for penance, led by the lord Kahenis of the water-buttressed town of Punt. They tell him it is nearly Good Friday and rebuke him gently for riding armed on the holiest days of the year; he answers, bitterly, that he has long since stopped counting holy days, having renounced the God whose mercy he no longer trusts. They point him, out of pure kindness he does not think he deserves, toward a hermit nearby who might ease his heart.
stops.quote: Since ever I bear Him hatred Whom they worship with lowly heart, and they look for His aid, Who ever hath turnèd His face from me.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Parzival's thought among the penitents

stops.name: Trevrizent's grotto, Good Friday: the confession
stops.campa: In the cave the pilgrims named, Parzival finds an old hermit in a hair shirt, Trevrizent, who turns out to be brother to Anfortas and to Herzeloyde both, his own uncle. Reading in his psalter the days that have vanished, the hermit tells him plainly that four years, six months, and three days have passed since a spear was lost from this grotto, the very spear Parzival took unknowing from this same cave after the Orilus fight. Parzival confesses everything: the silence at the Grail table, the years of blind roaming, the hatred he has nursed against a God he no longer prays to.
stops.quote: It was Taurian, quoth the hermit, who his spear in my care did leave... four years and a half and three days shall have passed since we lost the spear.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Trevrizent's grotto, Easter: the teaching and the going forth
stops.campa: Through Holy Week and Easter, Trevrizent unfolds to his nephew the whole hidden history he has never heard: that the Grail is a stone, not a cup, borne by angels neutral in Heaven's old war and given since to a chosen family of guardians; that Anfortas's wound is punishment for a sin of pride in love, curable only by the compassionate question Parzival once failed to ask; and that God's mercy, far from having abandoned him, has been waiting the whole six years for him to stop cursing it. On the seventh of April Parzival rides out again reconciled, no longer a fool but not yet a king.
stops.quote: Sir Knight, thou shalt put away such madness, and trust God better, for His help will He never stay.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book IX, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Trevrizent to Parzival

stops.name: Joflanze (the Kembs plain), the camp of kings assembles
stops.campa: On the great sheep-plain the country calls Schofland, opposite the rock of Isteiner Klotz on the German shore, King Arthur's whole train arrives from Beaune to make good Gawain's promise of a duel with Gramoflanz over a garland won from a fatal tree. Tents rise for Arthur, for Orgeluse, for Gramoflanz's own army marching from Mülhausen; among the throng of unbadged knights drawn to any gathering of arms rides Parzival, once again unrecognized, once again about to collide with people he loves before he knows their faces in the press of tents and banners.

stops.name: Mönchsberg, the duel with an unknown knight
stops.campa: On the plateau above Mülhausen, near the old Roman road and the watchtower, Parzival and a knight he has never met fight to a standstill neither can explain, matching stroke for stroke until both are near collapse and their weapons are shattered in each other's hands. Only when the fight is broken off by onlookers does it emerge, to the astonishment and joy of both, that the stranger is Gawain, the same friend who once lifted the blood-trance from him on the Birs. They embrace where moments before they meant to kill each other, and ride together into camp as brothers again.
stops.quote: But he cast from his hand his weapon, and he cried, as he wept full sore, 'Accursèd am I, and dishonoured, and all blessing from me hath flown, since my luckless hand, unwitting, so sinful a strife hath known.'
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XIV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Parzival on learning his foe is Gawain

stops.name: Illberg, the garland and the duel with Gramoflanz
stops.campa: At the lime tree on the Illberg above the perilous ford of the Ill, the same tree whose garland Gawain won and whose owner Gramoflanz demanded satisfaction for, Parzival takes up his friend's unfinished quarrel and fights the king of Rosche Sabins to a standstill in his place, since Gawain's own wounds and Orgeluse's grief have made a substitute necessary. Arthur, arriving with his whole camp from Bems, brokers a peace between the households before more blood is spilled over a wreath of leaves, and the field that nearly hosted a third funeral instead hosts a wedding feast for Gramoflanz and Gawain's sister Itonje.
